interviewQuestions.question: Implement in-place run-length compression of a character array — encode runs of repeated characters as char+count.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd use two cursors over the same buffer: a read cursor that scans ahead to find the extent of each run, and a write cursor, always at or behind it, that commits the encoded output for that run once its full length is known.

First, since strings are immutable, I'd convert to a mutable character array — that's the precondition for any in-place work here.

```python
def compress(chars):
    write = read = 0
    n = len(chars)
    while read < n:
        char = chars[read]
        count = 0
        while read < n and chars[read] == char:
            read += 1
            count += 1
        chars[write] = char
        write += 1
        if count > 1:
            for digit in str(count):
                chars[write] = digit
                write += 1
    return write  # new logical length
```

Two details matter for correctness: a run's full count has to be known before anything is written for it, so read fully consumes the run first; and a count of 10 or more needs multiple output slots, so I write it digit by digit rather than assuming one character holds the whole count.

This is O(n) time — every character read exactly once — and O(1) extra space, since the write cursor never needs to allocate anything beyond the input buffer.

**Testing:** whether you get the read-before-write ordering and the multi-digit count right without being prompted for either.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: Why must the write cursor never advance past the read cursor in an in-place compression algorithm?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Because the read cursor is the only thing that knows what the original, un-corrupted data actually was — once the write cursor writes past the read cursor's current position, it's overwriting characters that haven't been examined yet, feeding the rest of the scan data that's already wrong.

Concretely: if a run's encoded form ever needs more slots than the run itself occupied in the original buffer — which can happen for very short runs, since a length-1 run consumes 1 slot but its encoded form (`char + "1"`) needs 2 — the write cursor can end up ahead of the read cursor. From that point on, the read cursor is scanning characters the write cursor already overwrote, not the real input, and the algorithm silently produces wrong output with no error raised anywhere.

This is exactly why the interview version of this problem checks the compressed length against the original before committing to it — for a string with mostly short runs, blind compression can actually make output longer than input, which is precisely the scenario where the write-overtakes-read risk shows up in the first place. Guaranteeing `write <= read` at every step of the algorithm is the correctness invariant the whole in-place approach depends on; without it, in-place isn't just an optimization detail, it's a bug waiting on the wrong input shape.

**Testing:** whether you can name the actual invariant an in-place two-cursor algorithm depends on, not just implement the happy path.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Correctness

interviewQuestions.question: How does this read-cursor/write-cursor pattern relate to other array techniques you know?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It's the same skeleton as a whole family of in-place array problems: a fast pointer that scans and decides what's real, and a slow pointer that only advances when there's something confirmed to commit — the two pointers move at different, decision-dependent rates rather than in lockstep.

Removing duplicates from a sorted array in place uses exactly this shape: read scans forward looking for the next distinct value, write commits it and advances only then. Moving all zeroes to the end while preserving relative order of non-zeroes does the same thing with a different "keep this or not" rule. This compression problem adds one more twist — write sometimes commits *more* than one output element per read decision (the count's digits), but the core discipline is identical: read decides, write commits, write never outruns read.

I'd contrast this with the two-pointer reversal technique elsewhere in this group, which converges from both ends toward the middle — a genuinely different two-pointer shape (symmetric, equal-rate) from this one (asymmetric, read-ahead-of-write). Recognizing which of the two shapes a new problem calls for — converging pointers vs. a lagging write cursor — is usually the fastest way into an unfamiliar in-place array problem, because it tells you immediately what invariant to maintain.

**Testing:** whether you see this as an instance of a general pattern rather than a memorized, one-off trick.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Pattern recognition

interviewQuestions.question: Your team is considering run-length encoding to shrink storage for a large text log file. Is that a good idea?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Almost certainly not for general text, and I'd explain why rather than just saying no. Run-length encoding only compresses well when the data has long runs of the *exact same character* repeated consecutively — sparse bitmaps, simple image formats, or a database column that repeats one value across many consecutive rows. English text and source code essentially never have runs of 3+ identical characters back to back, so RLE applied to a log file would do close to nothing, and for the many single-character "runs" (length 1 or 2), it can actually make the file *larger* — each of those encodes to 2 characters instead of 1.

What actually compresses general text well is exploiting repeated *patterns*, not repeated *single characters* — which is why production compressors (gzip, zstd) use dictionary-based back-references (LZ77-style matching of repeated substrings anywhere in a sliding window) combined with entropy coding (Huffman or arithmetic coding, which assigns shorter codes to more frequent characters/symbols). Those techniques compress a typical log file 3-10x; naive RLE on the same file would likely be a no-op or a net loss.

My recommendation: use an existing general-purpose compressor (gzip is nearly always available and good enough) rather than reaching for RLE, unless the specific field has genuinely long literal runs — e.g., a status column that's the same value across a long batch, which is a real, narrower use case RLE is still good at inside things like columnar storage formats.

**Testing:** whether you can reason about when a specific compression technique's assumptions match real data, rather than treating "compression" as one interchangeable idea.
